chunks: As for the hadith narrated by — Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Bazi', who said:

I asked al-Ridha (peace be upon him) about madhy, and he ordered me to perform wudu on account of it. Then I returned to him in another year and asked again, and he ordered me to perform wudu on account of it, and he said: 'Indeed, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib [variant: 'Aliyyan] (peace be upon him) ordered al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad to ask the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), but he ['Ali] felt too shy to ask him [directly], and he [the Prophet] said: "Wudu is required for it."'

This is a weak, anomalous report. What clarifies this is the aforementioned hadith narrated by Ishaq ibn 'Ammar from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him), which mentioned the story of Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) with al-Miqdad, and that when he [al-Miqdad] asked the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) about that, he [the Prophet] said: 'There is no harm in it.' Furthermore, this very same narrator has himself transmitted that it is permissible to omit wudu [after] madhy. It is therefore established thereby that the intent of the report is a form of recommendation [istihbab, not obligation].

key_terms.اَلاِسْتِحْبَابِ: istihbab — juridical recommendation; a commendable but non-obligatory act, contrasted with wujub (obligation)
key_terms.اَلْمَذْيِ: madhy — pre-seminal fluid; its status as a ritual impurity is a contested jurisprudential issue
key_terms.شَاذٌّ: shadhdh — anomalous; a narration that contradicts more widespread and authoritative transmissions
key_terms.ضَعِيفٌ: da'if — weak; technical hadith-criticism term denoting a narration with defects in its chain (sanad) or text (matn)

ai.seo_question: Does madhy necessitate wudu in Shia jurisprudence, and how did Shaykh al-Tusi evaluate the hadith of Ibn Bazi' from Imam al-Ridha (AS) in Tahdhib al-Ahkam?
ai.summary: This passage from Tahdhib al-Ahkam presents a hadith narrated by Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Bazi', in which Imam al-Ridha (AS) twice ordered wudu after madhy (pre-seminal fluid), citing a tradition tracing back via 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (AS) and al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad to the Prophet (SAWW). Shaykh al-Tusi then subjects this hadith to critical scrutiny, classifying it as weak (da'if) and anomalous (shadhdh), and reconciles it with a stronger narration of Ishaq ibn 'Ammar from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) — which states 'no harm in it' — concluding that wudu after madhy is merely recommended (mustahabb), not obligatory.
